The deck auto-sizes to the screens' footprint. Displays sit on the deck while it's shown, otherwise directly on the floor.

A preset replaces the current layout (save first if you need it). Cube and ribbon faces wrap around the arena, so they overlap in the 2D elevation — open the 3D view to see the ring. All presets use 500 × 500 mm P2.6 cabinets; adjust any screen afterwards as usual, and re-export.

View mode is look-only. In Edit mode, drag a display on the floor — sideways syncs to the 2D layout; forward / back is depth (Z), 3D-only. The floor is height 0 — nothing can go below it.

The camera icons are view cubes, like 3ds Max and Blender — the solid face is the side you look from. Front / Top / Left / Right are flat orthographic views. Free is the full camera — drag to orbit, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom.

Shaded shows each screen in its chosen colour, as a colour / lighter-colour chessboard like the 2D view. Flat turns the walls into a signal / port map — every cabinet in its flat port colour with its port number — and draws the rest of the stage in flat tones. Wireframe draws edges only. View modes only; they never change the layout. For a finished picture, press Render next to 3D View in the top bar.

Not connected

Independent (the default) — not connected: the two layouts are fully separate. Moving, rotating or resizing a wall in 3D changes only the 3D stage; editing in 2D never rearranges the 3D stage. The 2D layout stays the source of truth for cabling, ports and the PNG — so an arena 360 preset stays a long strip in 2D and a ring in 3D.

Technical

The whole stage as a 3D model, in metres: every cabinet an extruded box with its port colour on the front face, including bends, stacking, depth (Z) and preview tilts, plus the stage deck. Every format also carries a UV map of the front faces spanning the whole 2D layout — the layout is the UV map — so content made to the layout's pixel size (or your exported PNG's layout area) drops straight onto the walls in Blender, Twinmotion, Cinema 4D or Unreal. FBX is written in centimetres (the FBX standard unit) as an ASCII file.

LUTAS LED

A multi-screen LED layout and signal-mapping tool in the browser, laid out like the graphics editors you already know — tools on the left, canvas in the centre, settings and layers on the right.

Build a layout from one or many LED displays, set each screen's cabinet size and pixel pitch, choose its feed corner and cable path, and let data ports split automatically (numbers continue across displays). Move, rotate and scale displays directly on the canvas — scaling adds or removes cabinets, so panel counts, resolution, power, weight and ports always match the drawing. Export the finished layout as a PNG at its actual pixel size for the video crew, plus a cabling CSV and a copyable spec sheet. The 3D View — switched with the highlighted 2D View / 3D View toggle at the top of the window, where the top Export PNG button used to sit — stands the same layout on a real stage: extruded cabinets on an auto-sized deck, the floor locked at height 0, an orbit camera, an Edit mode for dragging displays, and walls that bend in flat sections — standing the same screens the 2D layout draws. In 3D, displays can also be stacked on top of each other and shifted in depth (Z) towards or away from the audience, without disturbing the accurate 2D layout. Both views have a transform gizmo on the selected display: in 2D a centre hub, red X / green Y axis arrows and a dashed rotate ring; in 3D Edit mode, red / green / blue move arrows, two-axis plane squares, rotate rings and a Blender-style Scale mode — axis cubes (red X scales the width, green Y the height, both in whole cabinets; blue Z and the white centre cube scale the wall uniformly; a blue square scales width + height together) — the red X and blue Z rotate rings are 3D-only tilts, and everything arranged in 3D follows the Layout Link setting (3D tab): Independent (the default, the broken-chain icon) keeps the two layouts fully separate — moving, rotating or resizing a wall in 3D changes only the 3D stage, and editing in 2D never rearranges the 3D stage, so an arena ring stays a long strip in 2D; Linked (the chain icon) connects them into one shared layout, so a 3D move, rotation or resize writes the real 2D position, degree and cabinet count, and resolution, ports, power and weight follow. And any single cabinet can carry a custom pixel resolution: select it with the Inspect tool and set its pixel size in the Cabinet Detail strip. The magnet (snap) strength is adjustable, the Render view's Simulator panel plays built-in VJ visuals, a shared Resolume window or an uploaded image or video across the whole layout so you can check content before the show — the simulator engine runs in the Render view only — stage presets in the Screens tab build centre-hung cube, ribbon-ring and end-stage + delay layouts in one click, the Export tab downloads a Clean PNG and a layered PSD at actual size, plus a Technical PDF — plus the stage as a 3D model (GLB, glTF, OBJ or FBX) — with a UV map matching the 2D layout, so layout content drops straight onto the walls — for previs in Blender or Twinmotion. In 3D every display pivots on its own centre, and the magnet strength pops up next to the magnet button in the 3D bar when you press it. The left rail is a Blender-style tool shelf — Hand, Position, Scale, Rotate, Shape edit, Bend and Inspect in one flat strip, with the View toggles under it and no zoom slider (zoom is the scroll wheel, a two-finger pinch, or Fit) — and the Window menu carries the same tools and the view options as their own sections, separate from its Layout panels list. In the 2D view, screens may not overlap silently: if a move, rotation, scale, duplicate or newly added screen would overlap another screen at the same height, it turns red while you drag and a message pops up when you let go, asking whether the overlap is OK — saying no puts the screen back where it was. Screens deliberately stacked on top of each other in 3D share a 2D footprint on purpose (they sit at different heights), so stacking never triggers the warning. On touch screens, the 2D view also zooms with a two-finger pinch — spreading or closing your fingers zooms around the point between them, and sliding both fingers pans — alongside the scroll wheel. The interface itself stays clean: Data & Stats is not a permanent panel — it sits in the Window menu and pops up as a window when clicked, alongside the Signal panel, which moved out of the settings tabs into the same Window menu, whose Layout panels list also shows or hides the Screens, 3D, Modifier, Export, Simulator and Layers panels — and the Edit menu carries Undo and Redo, which step back and forward through the last 5 changes to the layout (displays and modifiers), from the menu or with Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y — and File → Preferences opens a Preferences window — not a tab — holding the layout and interface settings: light / dark / auto theme, the measurement units the 3D measurements read in, learning mode (which brings back all the guidance and how-to notes that are otherwise hidden), and toggles for the canvas helpers (stage title chip, port legend, cabinet detail strip, dot grid). The panel list also includes bendable panels, modelled the way they really bend: flexible soft modules (320 × 160, 240 × 120 and 250 × 250) curve as one continuous arc set by a bend radius that can never go below the module's minimum, staying thin (about 10 mm) with the 2D width as the true arc length and the 3D footprint as the chord; curve-lock rigid cabinets (Absen, ROE and MSC types) stay flat and angle only at the joints between cabinets, within each type's per-joint limit for the bend direction — so their curves are faceted, exactly like the hardware. Bending never changes panel count, resolution, ports or cabling in any mode. The Modifier tab dresses the 3D stage with a 3ds Max-style modifier stack: add a Crowd (a standing concert crowd or a seated corporate audience), Lighting beams, a Truss, speaker stacks or Haze from the Modifier List, then select the modifier in the stack to edit its rollouts — modifiers appear on the 3D stage only and save with the layout. The Modifier List also has Props: your own imported 3D models (GLB works best; glTF, OBJ and best-effort FBX too), placed on the stage with the same gizmo — 3D and Render views only, never in the 2D layout or any screen export; files up to 3 MB embed in the layout JSON so they reopen in place, and a bigger file is flagged in its panel card rather than lost silently. A custom truss starts from the Custom section of the Truss modifier: its yellow Edit button is a mode toggle — press it and truss editing turns on: the current rig becomes your own editable segments, the truss tool comes up — a small icons-only toolbar at the bottom of the 3D canvas (add segment, draw path, delete the selected segment, clear all) — and in the 3D view only the truss can be moved or edited while the screens are locked; press Edit again and truss editing turns off, the toolbar and the truss handles go away, the truss locks, and the screens can be edited again. The toolbar is shown in 3D Edit mode only, staying hidden in View mode like the gizmo, and not there at all while truss editing is off. Its segments are listed in a Layers panel in the Modifier tab, Photoshop-style — each layer is just a name with a remove button, with icons-only add-truss and delete buttons on top of the panel — with the selected segment sleeved in amber so Delete always names its target; each segment's start point is a gray ball and its extend point a green ball — drag the green ball to extend the truss from its gray start — and the selected segment carries its own truss gizmo at its centre (Move arrows on all three axes plus a centre ball, a green Rotate ring, a Scale cube); the gizmo's three modes also drive the custom-build objects in 3D Edit mode: a truss segment drag moves it, Rotate mode yaws it about its centre, Scale mode stretches it about its centre, and a light fixture drag moves it, Rotate aims it (pan / tilt), Scale resizes the fixture and its beam. The Truss modifier is a full LED-wall support system, modelled on real rigging practice: choose Flown (beam above the wall, hanging bar, hoists to roof points), Goalpost (towers and a beam, load to the floor) or Ground-stacked (cabinets on a base bar, truss columns behind the wall with back clamps, rear braces, base plates and ballast), pick box, triangular or ladder truss, and the panel runs a live load check from the layout's real cabinet weights — total suspended weight, load per pickup against the hoist WLL you enter, and beam load against the published span table where the research carries one — flagging blockers (overloaded hoists, spans beyond the table, stacked walls without ballast, outdoor rigs without a design wind speed) as Not Approved rather than approximately OK, with a pre-hang checklist and the rigging written into the spec sheet. No number in it replaces the cabinet and truss datasheets or a qualified rigger's sign-off. The 3D camera bar adds Front / Top / Left / Right orthographic views — flat elevations and a plan with no perspective — plus a Free camera with full Blender-style control (orbit, tilt all the way over, screen-plane pan, dolly, and orbit / tilt / distance / target sliders in the 3D tab). The Lighting modifier is kept simple, Blender-style: Add light asks for the type first (Beam, Spot, Wash or the BSW hybrid), the new light is created already selected with its own move gizmo in the 3D Edit view (coloured arrows move it on one axis, the white ball moves it freely), and each light\u2019s type, colour, position, aim and size are changed one light at a time in a plain list \u2014 while beam angle, strength, moving the whole rig together and beam sweep sit together under \u201cMore \u2014 all lights together\u201d. The Signal panel and Data & Stats live in the Window menu as pop-up windows. The View toolset also carries a human size reference — an average person, 1.7 m tall, standing beside the selected display in the 2D view, and in 3D the MAn_S human model — a real GLB figure embedded with the app, scaled to exactly 1.70 m tall whatever its native size, lit by the stage lights and casting a shadow, so it reads as a person standing in the scene from every camera, in the Render view too — standing on top of the stage deck beside the wall, toggled from the View section of the left rail or the Edit menu — so a wall's real size reads at a glance; it is a view helper only and never appears in any export. The same View toolset carries a Measurements toggle (ruler icon): in the 2D view it draws a width and height dimension line on every display, and in the 3D view it draws dimension lines and labels for every element — each wall's width and height, the stage deck's width, depth and height, and a W × H × D extent box for every truss, speaker, lighting and crowd modifier — and the unit those measurements read in (metres, feet, inches, centimetres or millimetres) is chosen in File → Preferences → Measurement units.

Signal Panel

Signal routing for the selected display — where its feed starts, the cable path through its cabinets, and how data ports split. Changes apply to the layout, cabling list and exports straight away.

Cabinets / port
Pixels / port

655,360 px is the common NovaStar / Colorlight loading limit for one Ethernet port at 60 Hz. Port numbers continue across displays — Screen 1 might use ports 1–5, Screen 2 continues at port 6 — so one processor patch list covers the whole layout.

Preferences

Layout & interface settings for the whole app. Preferences are saved with your layout (File → Save layout) and restored when you load it.

The unit used by every measurement the app draws: the Measurements display (the ruler toggle in the View toolset — dimension lines on every display in the 2D view and on every element of the 3D stage), the 2D dimension captions, and the human reference height label. (The Technical Document PDF always reads in metres, like a standard pixel-map report.) Change it here and every measurement updates.

Learning modeShow the additional information — guidance hints, explanations and how-to notes — across the panels and the canvas. Off by default, for a clean interface.
Stage title chipProject name and layout summary at the top-left of the canvas.
Port legendThe colour key for ports along the bottom of the canvas.
Cabinet detail stripThe bar under the canvas that shows the inspected cabinet's number, port and position.
Canvas dot gridThe dotted background grid on the stage canvas.

Screens overlap

Screen 2 overlaps Screen 1 in the 2D layout. Is this overlap OK?

In the 2D layout screens should sit side by side without overlapping — two screens on the same stage area usually means a placement mistake. Confirm only if you really want them to overlap.

Link the layouts?

Linked connects the two layouts into one shared layout.

Independent keeps the two layouts fully separate — the 2D strip stays exactly as drawn (the source of truth for cabling, ports and the PNG export) while the 3D stage arranges the same walls its own way. That is why arena, cube, bent and stacked layouts stay Independent.

Magnet strength
15° · 10 px

How hard the magnet pulls while snap is on (or Shift is held): weak 5° / 5 px · medium 15° / 10 px · strong 30° / 25 px · max 45° / 50 px. Applies to gizmo drags in 2D and 3D.

Bending never changes panel count, resolution, ports or cabling — only the shape on stage. The 2D view stays the accurate flat front elevation: its width is the wall's true surface length (the arc length for soft modules); the curved footprint shows in the 3D view. Soft modules bend along one axis only, like rolling a sheet — never across the rows.

PIVOTCentre · 50%

The pivot is the point the wall bends around — it stays put while the rest of the wall swings around it. Drag the amber diamond on the wall in the 2D view, or the amber ball on the wall in the 3D Edit view, to move it.
